verdicts.trueWording: he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix 'a-' to denote position
verdicts.note: Raw page (astrofella.wordpress.com, curl 200) reads: "delving beyond common speech into archaic native forms: for example, he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix 'a-' to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse". Quote byte-exact; every limb (archaic, native, prefix a-, position, atop/abed/ahorse) on the page, in section '1. The prefix'.

verdicts.trueWording: lexical choices as important as subject matter; brutal, archaic worldview
verdicts.note: Raw page Abstract: "then conclude that the lexical choices he makes are as important as the subject matter of the stories in creating the novels' brutal, archaic worldview." Quote byte-exact; 'concludes' and 'archaic worldview' both on the page. Located in the Abstract rather than the labelled Introduction, a locator detail only.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences
verdicts.note: Raw page (atseajournal.com, curl 200): "To that end, Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences." Byte-exact; the oral-vs-textual storytelling context matches the cited section.

verdicts.trueWording: It's shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective
verdicts.note: Raw page: "It's shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge of it gets the point across." Byte-exact including the curly apostrophe. The claim's 'no single sentence carries the effect on its own' matches; the page's completing clause (the full cartridge does) is compatible, not contradictory.

verdicts.trueWording: the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable
verdicts.note: Raw page, under the heading 'The con: The sentences aren't beautiful': top-voted favourite passages are all dialogue, "But the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable." 'the other 60%' is explicitly the non-dialogue remainder, so both limbs (60 percent share, forgettable) hold.

verdicts.trueWording: for a writer, they come easily off the pen; very important for momentum
verdicts.note: Raw page: "Which could be why stock phrases are so prevalent in his work... But for a writer, they come easily off the pen. Very important for maintaining momentum." preceded by "The flow is important". All limbs supported; the essayist's own framing is hedged ('could be why'), where the claim says 'argues'.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin knows just where to drop his periods
verdicts.note: Raw YouTube description (shortDescription, curl 200): "Martin knows just where to drop his periods, and is able to break up large descriptions into easily digestible sentences... help aspiring writers learn where to end their sentences". Byte-exact. The 'five-part series' limb is confirmed by the sibling raw pages I fetched: parts [1]-[5], same channel 'Corey Huffman - Writer', cross-linked; this page alone says only 'More to come'.

verdicts.trueWording: break up large descriptions into easily digestible sentences
verdicts.note: Same raw description: "is able to break up large descriptions into easily digestible sentences." Byte-exact; every limb on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: contrast allows him to accomplish multiple narrative tasks simultaneously
verdicts.note: Raw description of [2] (title '[2] The Prose of George R R Martin | Why You Should Contrast Your Descriptions'): "how Martin uses the literary technique of 'contrast' to enrich these descriptions, and how this technique allows him to accomplish multiple narrative tasks simultaneously." Byte-exact with curly quotes; 'several narrative jobs at once' matches 'multiple narrative tasks simultaneously'.

verdicts.trueWording: I examine twenty-five metaphors and similes... in A Game of Thrones
verdicts.note: Raw description of [3]: "In this video, I examine twenty-five metaphors and similes masterfully crafted by George R R Martin in his novel, 'A Game of Thrones.'" Byte-exact; part number, count and source novel all on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: he often uses "The Rule of 3" structuring adjectives, nouns, and clauses
verdicts.note: Raw description of [4]: "show how he often uses \"The Rule of 3\" with regards to structuring his adjectives, nouns, and clauses." Byte-exact; 'frequently' matches 'often', and the adjective/noun/clause triple is verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: how you, as a writer, can meld the two voices
verdicts.note: Quote byte-exact in the raw description of [5], and the A Clash of Kings limb holds ("using excerpts taken from George R R Martin's novel, 'A Clash of Kings'"). But the description attributes the melding to the reader-writer, not to Martin, and says the purpose is "to take your reader on a smooth, vivid, and immersive journey" - not a single narrative movement.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Martin himself melds the two voices 'within a single narrative movement' - the page frames melding as advice to the aspiring writer ('how you, as a writer, can meld the two voices') and never uses or paraphrases 'single narrative movement'

verdicts.trueWording: more successful than Rice's history more for what is left unsaid
verdicts.note: Raw page (sffworld.com, curl 200), Rob H. Bedford's Fevre Dream review: "I find it more successful than Rice's history more for what is left unsaid and told for Rice left seemingly no stone unturned. A little bit of mystery is stronger than knowing the full scope." Byte-exact; the preference over Anne Rice and the unsaid-as-reason limb both hold.

verdicts.trueWording: It lacks the elegant simplicity of The Hedge Knight
verdicts.note: Raw forum page (curl 200), post #1 headed 'The Mystery Knight': "It lacks the elegant simplicity of The Hedge Knight but isn't as slight as The Sworn Sword." Byte-exact. The page names the reviewer only by the handle 'Werthead' with the signature 'Visit The Wertzone for reviews of SF&F books' - it never prints 'Adam Whitehead', so the real-name attribution rests on the handle and blog signature.

verdicts.trueWording: an unusually neat ending by Martin's standards... lacks the messy consequences
verdicts.note: Same post: "the story lacks the satisfying conclusion of The Hedge Knight, with an unusually neat ending by Martin's standards (although the final line is superb) that lacks the messy consequences he usually favours." Byte-exact; both limbs (unusually neat for Martin, missing messy consequences) verbatim. Same handle caveat as 893.
